Newborn Steppe polecats (Mustela eversmanii) are remarkably altricial, weighing just 5.73 grams [Wwb = 5.73 grams] at birth. These tiny neonates develop rapidly within the protection of the maternal den. Females reach sexual maturity relatively early, with the onset of puberty occurring at 319 days since birth [tp = 319 days since birth], a life-history timing that reflects the species' strategy of capitalizing on fluctuating rodent prey populations at a temperature of 39 °C [T = 39 °C]. This comparatively early maturation allows young females to contribute to the next generation during the peak of the following breeding season. Field studies indicate that gestation proceeds for a period of 36 days [tg = 36 days] when the female maintains a body temperature of 39 °C [T = 39 °C], a thermal condition that is typical for the species during reproductive activity. The relatively brief gestation is characteristic of mustelids of this body size, allowing for multiple litters should the first be lost, and it represents a trade-off between offspring developmental stage at parturition and the energetic demands on the gravid female.

Within the thermally stable environment of the burrow, which is maintained near the species' core temperature of 39 °C [T = 39 °C], the weaning process begins at 51 days since birth [tx = 51 days since birth]. At this critical developmental juncture, the kits have reached a wet weight of approximately 110 grams [Wwx = approximately 110 grams], signaling the transition from complete reliance on milk to the integration of solid food brought by the mother. The nursing period represents a phase of intense energetic investment for the lactating female, whose metabolic machinery must sustain both milk production and her own basal maintenance. The timing of weaning aligns with the seasonal peak in vole and ground squirrel abundance, ensuring that newly independent juveniles encounter a landscape rich in accessible prey. This synchronization with food availability is a key determinant of juvenile survival rates in the semi-arid steppe ecosystems that this polecat inhabits.

Basal metabolic rate measurements for the Steppe polecat reveal an oxygen consumption of 434.5 milliliters per hour [JOi = 434.5 milliliters per hour] when the subject is at rest and thermoneutral at 39 °C [T = 39 °C]. This relatively elevated metabolic rate, compared to other mammals of a similar mass, is linked to the species' elongate, tubular body plan and high surface-area-to-volume ratio, which engenders greater heat loss. The energetic cost of maintaining endothermy in the cold, continental steppe climate is substantial, and the species must sustain high daily food intake to meet these demands. This physiological constraint has profound implications for the species' ecology, limiting its distribution to regions where rodent prey is consistently abundant. The measured rate provides a baseline for understanding the energetic budget of this active, pursuit-hunting mustelid.

Adult body size in this species exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism, a common pattern among mustelids. Ultimate wet weight for females is typically around 1400 grams [Wwi = around 1400 grams], while males attain a substantially larger ultimate wet weight of 2000 grams [Wwi = 2000 grams]. This size disparity is thought to result from sexual selection on male fighting ability during the breeding season, as larger males are better able to defend territories and gain access to receptive females. In contrast, the smaller body size of females may confer an energetic advantage, reducing total food requirements during the demanding period of gestation and lactation. The species exhibits a maximum lifespan of 9.1 years [am = 9.1 years] under the typical thermal conditions provided in captivity at 39 °C [T = 39 °C], though longevity in the wild is likely shorter due to predation and the rigors of seasonal resource fluctuations.

Reproductive output in the Steppe polecat is characterized by large litters that compensate for relatively high juvenile mortality. Females produce 9.4 pups per litter [N_R_i = 9.4 pups per litter], a remarkably high fecundity for a carnivore of this size, and they typically raise a single litter per year [F_R_i = single litter per year] under the species' optimal thermal conditions at 39 °C [T = 39 °C]. The high pup count allows for some offspring to survive despite the intense predation pressure from raptors and larger mammalian carnivores that target polecat dens. This annual reproductive schedule is keyed to the spring peak in prey abundance, ensuring that the demanding period of late lactation coincides with maximum food availability for provisioning mothers. The combination of a brief gestation, rapid juvenile growth, and high litter size underscores the species' classification as an r-selected strategist within the Mustelidae family.
